brief.headline: Oil and aluminium decoupled on Monday: Brent has now fallen three sessions in a row to about $87 as Washington and Tehran hold fire and mediators talk, yet the LME aluminium official went the OTHER way - cash $3,192.00 (+$17.00) and 3M $3,181.00 (+$20.50) - because a US Navy-overseen maritime body put commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz at a THREE-WEEK LOW and Iran's foreign ministry said plainly that there are no direct US-Iran talks and the waterway remains closed.
bullets: WHAT MOVED: the 27-Jul official - the first LME session to see the weekend - rose. Cash $3,192.00 (+$17.00, +0.54%), 3M $3,181.00 (+$20.50, +0.65%), and warehouse stock drew another 1,500 t to 271,275 t, a fresh low since 2022 and -46.7% YTD. But the cash-3M backwardation NARROWED to +$11.00 from +$14.50. That is the exact inverse of Friday's configuration, when price fell and the spread widened.

WHY: the two markets priced different things. Energy priced the diplomacy - Brent $87.25 (-0.78%), a third straight fall and roughly -11% from Friday's $98.38, after Trump said the US was in 'good talks' with Iran and both sides went three days without an attack. Aluminium priced the waterway instead: commercial traffic through Hormuz was at a three-week low on Sunday (fewer than 10 commodity ships passing Monday morning against roughly 100 a day pre-war), the US naval blockade is still running (a dozen ships redirected, two disabled, two boarded), and about 9% of global primary supply sits behind that strait.

THE DETAIL THAT MATTERS: the talks are not what the headline implies. Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson said mediators may pass messages but there are no direct negotiations with Washington, and that the strait remains closed; the live mechanism is a bilateral Iran-Oman arrangement for managing vessel transit, and Tehran still asserts a right to manage the waterway and potentially charge fees, which the US rejects. Qatar- and Pakistan-led mediation was described by one regional official as making 'significant' progress, but a transit mechanism is months from moving metal even if signed.

WATCH THIS WEEK: Netanyahu meets Trump in Washington today - the clearest live escalation vector against a three-day lull; whether the strike pause survives it; whether Hormuz transit counts recover off the three-week low or stay pinned; and whether the LME draw takes stock through 270,000 t while the backwardation keeps flattening. Price rising on a NARROWING spread is the first tentative sign that physical relief is being anticipated rather than positioning being squeezed - one session is not a trend.

drivers.text: US Section 232 at 50% - the tariff leg is ~66% of the US duty-paid premium and rose mechanically on Monday — Aluminium articles made entirely or almost entirely of aluminium pay 50% on full customs value (derivative aluminium content pays 25%); proclamation 01-Jun-2026, effective 08-Jun-2026 through 31-Dec-2027, CBP guidance CSMS #68855869 - re-verified this run, rate unchanged. At the 27-Jul cash of $3,192 that is ~$1,596.00/t of pure policy cost inside a ~$2,420/t duty-paid premium, leaving ~$824.00/t of residual market premium. Because the leg is a fixed percentage of the LME, Monday's $17 rise in cash added ~$8.50/t of tariff cost by arithmetic alone, with no change in policy or physical tightness. UK-origin metal is subject to 25% rather than 50%.
drivers.source: White & Case - United States modifies steel, aluminum and copper Section 232 tariffs

drivers.text: The energy leg of delivered cost has collapsed - Brent is down roughly 11% in two sessions — Brent fell to $87.25 on 28-Jul, a third consecutive session of losses and about 11% below the $98.38 settlement of 24-Jul, after Trump said the US was engaged in 'good talks' with Iran, both sides paused attacks for three days, and Caspian Pipeline Consortium loadings resumed on Russia's Black Sea coast. That is real relief in the freight, bunker and war-risk component embedded in every regional premium, and in the power cost of gas-exposed European and Asian smelters. It is also the clearest evidence that the energy market is discounting a settlement faster than the metal market, which is still pricing a strait that Iran says is closed.
drivers.source: Trading Economics - Brent Extends Fall as US-Iran Talks Resume (27/28-Jul-2026)

drivers.text: New US primary capacity remains a medium-term drag on the RESIDUAL US premium — Commerce and South Carolina officials marked Century Aluminum's Mt Holly expansion on 23-Jul, publicly framed as lifting total US domestic primary aluminium output by roughly 10%, with Magnitude 7 Metals restarting part of the New Madrid smelter in Missouri (~75 kt/y). Domestic units displace tariffed imports at the margin, which pressures the ~$824.00/t residual market leg of the US duty-paid premium while leaving the ~$1,596.00/t tariff leg entirely untouched. A July incentive program also lets approved companies investing in US primary capacity import tied metal at half the applicable rate.
drivers.source: GlobeNewswire - Commerce, Senator Scott and Governor McMaster mark ~10% increase in US aluminum production (23-Jul-2026)

notes: The alumina market remains the mirror image of metal: globally LOOSENING (EGA's 2.4 Mtpa Al Taweelah restart at full output since 10-Jul, record Guinean bauxite exports, Chinese port stocks building; SMM Alumina Index easing toward ~Y2,700/t) - ex-China consolidates at ~$300-322 (FOB Australia ~$322, API ~$300, Platts futures $309.40).

The delivered-cost wrinkle eased sharply on the energy leg but not the transit leg. Brent has fallen three sessions to $87.25, about 11% below Friday, and a maritime body overseen by the US Navy reports Bab el-Mandeb traffic 'remained steady' - both cheapen freight. But Hormuz commercial traffic was at a THREE-WEEK LOW on Sunday and Iran says the strait remains closed, so the war-risk cover embedded in the ~60% of Gulf alumina imports that transit it has not re-priced with crude. SMM separately flags ex-China metallurgical-grade output down ~6% y/y in June.

The ore leg still runs against the bull case: Guinea's H1-2026 exports hit a RECORD 114.8 Mt (+15% y/y), with China taking 82.57 Mt Jan-May (+24% y/y). Guinea's pending export-quota policy (a considered cap near 150 Mt for 2026, targeting >$100/dmt) remains undecreed, and the record H1 flow materially weakens the case for it biting in 2026.

logistics.label: Red Sea corridor
logistics.note: The Houthis threatened a blockade of Saudi-linked shipping and fired on at least one Saudi tanker, setting it alight, and claimed attacks on Aramco facilities at Jizan and Yanbu that neither Riyadh nor Aramco confirmed. Saudi Arabia separately shot down drones fired by Iran-backed militias in Iraq at its petroleum facilities. Despite that, the maritime body overseen by the US Navy reported traffic through Bab el-Mandeb 'remained steady' - a modest improvement on last week's read for Suez-routed metal, reagent and alumina. The corridor carries roughly 12% of world trade and became more important for Gulf exports precisely because Hormuz was disrupted, so it stays a live premium driver even while flowing.

logistics.label: Gulf / Red Sea war-risk insurance
logistics.note: War-risk quotes stay elevated with two fronts in play, but the premium is easing at the margin: Brent settled $98.38 on 24-Jul (-2.29%) off the $100+ spike, and the weekend brought a US pause in strikes plus constructive Iran-Oman talks on Hormuz safe passage. Retain elevated insurance, interdiction and deviation-risk assumptions in Gulf- and Red Sea-routed freight and delivered-cost models, but the skew on that cost line has turned lower for the first time in weeks.

logistics.note: Dry-bulk freight (a separate, slower-moving cost line) eased to ~2,671 on 20-Jul, down 81 points and off a mid-month peak near 2,944 on softer Capesize demand. Price the two legs separately: dry-bulk freight vs. the Gulf/Red Sea war-risk surcharge (Trading Economics / Baltic Exchange).

logistics.label: Land-bridge / alt routes (Gulf, Kazakh oil)
logistics.note: The overland-to-Red-Sea contingency is less clean with the Red Sea under attack. Separately, the Caspian Pipeline Consortium suspended loadings at its Black Sea terminal after tanker attacks, disrupting ~80% of Kazakhstan's oil exports - a reminder that alternative routes are also under stress. Keep carrier capacity and lead times current for any Gulf-origin cargo.

logistics.label: Incoterms / demurrage
logistics.note: Attacks spanning two waterways keep force-majeure and deviation clauses live for any Gulf- or Red Sea-routed cargo; war-risk surcharge pass-through and interdiction/delay risk remain live contract points to negotiate cargo-by-cargo. Generic supply-chain observation, not company-specific.

The move followed Trump's statement that the US is in 'good talks' with Iran, a three-day halt in strikes by both sides, Iran-Oman weekend negotiations on restoring Hormuz shipping, and the resumption of Caspian Pipeline Consortium loadings on Russia's Black Sea coast. Brent is still up ~18% on the month. Energy is the largest smelter cost line, so this is the single clearest cost relief in the current picture - and the sharpest evidence that the energy market is discounting a settlement faster than the metal market. (Trading Economics)

headlines.title: The 27-Jul official rose against a falling oil price: cash $3,192.00 (+$17.00) and 3M $3,181.00 (+$20.50), the firmest official 3M since 22-Jul, while stock drew a further 1,500 t to 271,275 t - another low since 2022 and -46.7% YTD. The cash-3M backwardation NARROWED to +$11.00 from +$14.50. Price up on a flatter spread is the inverse of Friday's configuration: the forward curve firmed faster than the prompt, which is what anticipation of eventual supply relief looks like rather than an intensifying squeeze.

Hormuz commercial traffic hit a THREE-WEEK LOW even as the shooting stopped. A maritime body overseen by the US Navy reported fewer than 10 commodity ships transiting on Monday morning against roughly 100 a day pre-war, with no new attacks confirmed in the prior 72 hours; Bab el-Mandeb traffic remained steady. Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson said there are no direct US-Iran negotiations - only a bilateral Iran-Oman track on managing vessel transit - and stressed the waterway remains closed. The physical constraint has not followed the diplomacy, and roughly 9% of global primary supply sits behind that route.

The de-escalation track is real but indirect. Qatar- and Pakistan-led mediators are working to return Washington and Tehran to the interim ceasefire that collapsed, with one regional official calling progress 'significant'; neither side reported an attack for three days, Trump said he suspended strikes to give talks room, and the US ambassador to the UN said he was 'giving talks some space'. Trump also warned the US would 'go back to doing what we were doing' if negotiations stall, and the naval blockade of Iranian ports continues with a dozen ships redirected, two disabled and two boarded.

Brent fell to $87.25 on 28-Jul, a third consecutive session of losses and roughly 11% below the $98.38 settlement of 24-Jul, after Trump's 'good talks' comment, the halt in strikes, Iran-Oman weekend negotiations on restoring Hormuz shipping, and the resumption of Caspian Pipeline Consortium loadings on Russia's Black Sea coast. Crude is still up about 18% on the month. Energy is the largest smelter cost line, so the collapse in the crude war-risk premium is material relief for gas-exposed European and Asian producers - and the sharpest evidence that the energy market is discounting a settlement faster than the metal market.
headlines.source: Trading Economics - Brent Extends Fall as US-Iran Talks Resume (28-Jul-2026)

headlines.title: Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu meets Trump in Washington on Tuesday 28-Jul, their first Washington meeting since February, weeks before the war on Iran began. Israel has been absent from the renewed US strikes, so its re-entry would be a material escalation against the current three-day lull. Around the lull, Saudi Arabia shot down drones fired by Iran-backed militias in Iraq at its petroleum facilities and the Houthis claimed attacks on Saudi oil facilities at Jizan and Yanbu, unconfirmed by Riyadh or Aramco.

The supply-side counterweights keep compounding: EGA's 2.4 Mtpa Al Taweelah alumina refinery has been at full output since 10-Jul after a three-and-a-half-month outage, ex-China alumina consolidates at ~$300-322 with Platts FOB Australia futures at $309.40, Guinea shipped a record 114.8 Mt of bauxite in H1-2026 (+15% y/y), and new US primary units are coming behind the tariff wall - Century's Mt Holly expansion, publicly framed as roughly +10% of US domestic primary output, plus a partial New Madrid restart.

Section 232 on aluminium is unchanged and re-verified this run: 50% on full customs value for articles made entirely or almost entirely of aluminium, 25% on derivative aluminium content, effective 08-Jun-2026 through 31-Dec-2027 (proclamation 01-Jun-2026; CBP guidance CSMS #68855869), with UK-origin metal at 25%. Because the leg is a fixed percentage of the LME, Monday's $17 rise in cash mechanically added about $8.50/t to the US duty-paid premium with no change in policy or physical tightness.
headlines.source: White & Case - US modifies steel, aluminum and copper Section 232 tariffs

forward.basis: LME official prices via Westmetall. Baseline = LME 3-month official (a traded market price). Range = random-walk cone from realized volatility. Driver score = 3 transparent rules, hit rate measured on history.
forward.source: London Metal Exchange official settlements via Westmetall (https://www.westmetall.com/en/markdaten.php?action=table&field=LME_Al_cash)
forward.stance_label: Current physical-market condition (diagnostic, not a forecast)

drivers.name: Curve carry (cash − 3M)
drivers.rule: Backwardation (cash above 3M) = prompt physical tightness = bullish; contango = bearish.

drivers.name: Inventory trend (13-week)
drivers.rule: LME stock falling more than 2% over 13 weeks = tightening = bullish; rising >2% = bearish.

drivers.name: Momentum (3M vs 20-week average)
drivers.rule: Price above its 20-week average = uptrend = bullish; below = bearish.

backtest.verdict: These condition indicators showed NO predictive edge when tested: a 39.2% directional hit rate against a 72.5% naive 'always higher' baseline over the same sample, and forward returns after 'tightening' readings averaged 2.09% versus 7.04% after 'loosening' readings. They are therefore published as a read on CURRENT market condition only — not as a price forecast. The forward baseline and probability range above are the forward-looking view.
backtest.caveat: Measured on overlapping 13-week windows of weekly LME data (97 observations, 2024-05-24 to 2026-05-01). Overlapping windows overstate significance and the sample spans a single, largely rising market — evidence in either direction is weak.

earnings.note: Q2 2026 BEAT: adjusted EBITDA NOK 8,923m (+14.5% y/y vs NOK 7,790m; above consensus); Aluminium Metal adjusted EBITDA NOK 6,421m; adjusted EPS NOK 2.2 (from NOK 1.7); free cash flow NOK 4bn; 12-month adjusted RoaCE 10.9%. Shares rose on the print. First European producer P&L of the Hormuz-disruption quarter. Higher aluminium prices and product premiums plus stronger recycling earnings drove the beat; a stronger NOK and lower hydro-power output were partial offsets. Confirms the disruption-quarter price/premium is translating into real producer margin - a positive read-across for the smelter complex.

June-quarter production report: Worsley alumina 943 kt, Hillside aluminium 179 kt; group beat FY26 production guidance with quarterly sales +15%. Sale of the aluminium value chain to Alcoa (announced 01-Jul) progressing. Upstream volumes intact and above guidance; the aluminium/alumina divestment to Alcoa repositions S32 as an upstream base-metals play. Confirms Western supply is expressing the Gulf disruption through price/freight, not lost tonnage.

Revenue $3.97bn (+24% q/q, highest in nearly a decade); adj. EPS $2.12 (MISS vs ~$2.31 consensus); adj. net income $562m; adj. EBITDA $901m (from $595m in Q1); Aluminum segment RECORD EBITDA $1.073bn at 32.3% margin. First producer P&L under the Hormuz-disruption regime: record aluminium margins and near-decade-high revenue on higher LME + strong US Midwest premiums, but adj. EPS missed on higher costs — notably ~$35m more Section-232 tariff on Canadian metal into the US — and the shares fell. South32 upstream acquisition ($4.1bn upfront, up to $5.6bn contingent to 2030) progressing, close expected H1-2027. The tariff is a double edge: it inflates US premia but taxes Alcoa's cross-border Canadian metal.

Q2 2026 production (14-Jul): aluminium 841 kt (flat y/y, +1% q/q); bauxite recovered from Q1 weather; alumina reduced q/q on Yarwun/Vaudreuil reliability events; group aluminium guidance intact 3.25-3.45 Mt. Kitimat, NZAS and AP60 continued their ramp-up while Arvida's final two potlines closed in June as planned, completing the transition to AP60. Steady low-carbon Canadian output into a tight, premium-rich market - constructive for realised margins even as the flat price eased.

Guides H1-26 net profit ¥1.8–1.95bn, +154.4–175.6% YoY. Credits industry-chain cost reduction, aluminium prices fluctuating at highs, high-value-added deep-processing mix and energy-saving retrofits — the first sizeable China H1 pre-announcement of the season and a positive read-across for Chinese producer margins.

Hindalco PAT ₹5,283cr (+66% YoY); India Al upstream EBITDA margin ~46%; Novelis FY26 adj. EBITDA $1.6bn (−9%). Record India operations; Novelis pressured by Oswego outage (~$104m) and tariffs (~$143m).

caveats: Report refreshed Tue 28-Jul-2026, ~06:05 London - BEFORE the LME ring. The benchmark table and lme_series carry the latest PUBLISHED LME aluminium official, which is the 27-Jul (Monday) settlement: cash $3,192.00 / 3M $3,181.00 / stock 271,275 t, from Westmetall, re-verified against the source at this refresh. Today's official prints 13:20 London, so nothing in this report reflects Tuesday's session - including Netanyahu's Washington meeting, which takes place today.

SOURCE-CACHE NOTE: on the first request this run, Westmetall returned a cached page whose newest row was still 24-Jul. A cache-busted request returned the 27-Jul row for aluminium, copper, nickel, zinc and lead. Every figure published here is taken from the cache-busted response and was cross-checked for internal consistency against the prior session's values.

BOARD BASIS IS UNIFORM: aluminium, copper, nickel, zinc and lead are all set to their LME 27-Jul 3-month officials (Westmetall), each re-verified this run - a single, consistent session across the whole board. Spot/CFD references (Trading Economics) are a different basis from officials and will not tie out exactly: the traded aluminium reference closed $3,168.35 on 27-Jul against the official 3M of $3,181.00, and Trading Economics' nickel ($17,370.38) and zinc ($3,619.95) differ from the LME officials shown.

YTD FIGURES ON THE BOARD are computed against each metal's first-published 2026 LME 3-month official (aluminium: $3,010.50 on 02-Jan-2026; copper $12,511.00; nickel $16,915.00; zinc $3,130.50; lead $2,008.00) and are indicative, derived figures - not exchange-published index returns. Aluminium's -46.7% YTD stock change is measured from 509,250 t on 02-Jan-2026.

PRICE AND ENERGY DIVERGED THIS SESSION and the report says so explicitly: Brent's 28-Jul level ($87.25) is one day FRESHER than the 27-Jul LME official it is discussed alongside. That basis gap is deliberate and disclosed - crude trades continuously while LME officials print once a day at 13:20 London - but it means the oil-versus-metal divergence described here spans two different observation times.

PREMIUM ASSESSMENTS ARE PERIODIC, NOT DAILY. MJP is a quarterly settlement (Q3-2026 at $395/t, assessed 06-Jul); Rotterdam duty-unpaid carries a 03-Jul public mid; US Midwest duty-paid is an SMM weekly at 10-Jul; billet is a late-June reference. Where no fresher public print exists the last public mark is carried forward with its assessment date labelled rather than implying a daily move. The ONLY premium component recomputed every run is the Section-232 decomposition, because it is a fixed percentage of the current LME cash.

ALUMINA AND RAW-MATERIAL MARKS are likewise periodic and several carry pre-28-Jul assessment dates (Platts FOB Australia futures 24-Jul; ex-China API mid-Jul; FOB WA and SMM index late-Jul; caustic Q2). Fastmarkets and Platts daily assessments are not published free of charge, so the public marks shown are the freshest that can be sourced and attributed openly.

GEOPOLITICAL DEVELOPMENTS ARE FAST-MOVING AND THE TWO NARRATIVES CONFLICT. The diplomatic track improved (three days without attacks, Qatar/Pakistan-led mediation described as making 'significant' progress, Trump's 'good talks' remark) while the physical track deteriorated (Hormuz commercial transits at a three-week low, Iran stating the strait remains closed and that there are no direct US-Iran negotiations, the naval blockade continuing). Both are reported here because both are true and they carry opposite price implications; readers should not treat either as settled.

ELLIOTT WAVE CONTENT IS TECHNICAL CONTEXT, NOT ADVICE. Wave counts are interpretive, alternative counts exist, and the stated invalidation levels are the discipline that governs them. The 27-Jul session added one confirmed bar; the weekly count is unchanged and the daily count is carried forward with the wave (ii) low at $3,175 intact.

EVERYTHING PUBLISHED HERE IS PUBLIC, SOURCED MARKET INFORMATION for situational awareness only. No confidential, internal or company-specific data is included, and nothing here constitutes trading, hedging, commercial or investment advice. The only company references are public listed-company disclosures in the peer-earnings table.
